newsitem.title: HUNGARY: FEATURE - Hungary veers right but no Le Pen, please.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Hungary veers right but no Le Pen, please.

text.p: Hungarian political sentiment has taken a sharp turn to the right in a non-election year, but the last thing leading conservatives want to hear about is Jean-Marie Le Pen and other right-wing European radicals.
"We have absolutely no connection with Le Pen nor with other (radical rightists)," said Jozsef Torgyan, the 64-year-old, sharp-tongued president of the Smallholders Party.

The Smallholders, a 90-year-old party which draws its strength from peasant farmers and the poor or lower-middle class, are running neck and neck in opinion polls with the youth-oriented Budapest-based Fidesz, which once barred membership to anyone over 35.

Both have gained at the expense of the ruling coalition of Socialists and liberal Free Democrats, hurt by a scandal over illegal payments to a privatisation consultant, discontent over falling real wages and widespread agrarian protests.
A poll by the respected Szonda-Ipsos firm, showed the Smallholders were backed by 29 percent of those questioned, Fidesz by 24, the Socialists by 22 and the Free Democrats by eight.
Parliamentary elections are still more than a year off, but already the political jockeying has begun.
"Prime Minister (Gyula) Horn should resign and parliament be dissolved so we can hold early elections," Torgyan told Reuters. "This would satisfy the population and calm them down."

"It is clear that the illusion that the old post-communist comrades (the Socialists) coming back to power could improve the economy and social life -- has disappeared," said Fidesz leader Viktor Orban, a party founder in 1989 who has stayed to see the age limit lifted now that he is 34.
"One decision in the spirit of the country has already been made and that is that we would like to get rid of them...The question is who will replace them, and this is an open question," Orban added.
RULING COALITION VULNERABLE
The surge in popularity for the right and centre-right comes at a time when the ruling coalition is particularly vulnerable, political analysts said.

The coalition's popularity began to crumble late last year with a scandal surrounding the illegal payment of some 800 million forints ($5 million) to consultant Marta Tocsik, forcing a huge overhaul of the privatisation agency APV Rt and the sacking of the privatisation minister.
"They (the coalition) badly mishandled the so-called Tocsik affair," said political consultant Tibor Vidos. "And basically there is already a strong trend against politicians in power.

"It looked like people who were close to the Socialists were trying to cover up things...and in a normal democracy when things like this happen heads roll extremely quickly. Here it didn't happen like that and some heads didn't roll at all."

The government, in power since 1994, only recently unveiled a draft agricultural policy to help the stricken farm sector. Some farmer groups, angered by delay and the vagueness of the plan, have mounted road and border blockades to express their anger.
"The Horn government, in the fourth year of rule, has just discovered now that they have no agricultural policy and now suddenly they start one," Torgyan said.

"But this dilettante, untalented government can have no results," he added. "And it is not just the farmers who are protesting, it is the doctors, the teachers, the nurses, the firemen, the sick people, the trade unions, the retired people...Hungary is in a general crisis situation."

But neither Orban nor Torgyan, who has a reputation as a populist orator who stirred up controversy with remarks in a 1996 National Day speech about "pseudo-liberal worms and disgusting vultures" in the Horn government, want to claim any kinship to France's Le Pen or other European far-rightists.
STRONG BACKING FOR NATIO, EU MEMBERSHIP
Unlike Euro-sceptics such as Le Pen, or Austria's Joerg Haider, Orban and Torgyan strongly back Hungary's candidacy for entry into NATO and the European Union as quickly as possible.
"I am very much in favour of EU membership, but it's obvious that there will be many people who will lose in the short term from Hungary becoming a member," Orban said.

"It stands to reason that the more radical parties will see this as a political chance -- to represent the losers of enlargement," he said, adding that as leader of a Hungarian government he would cut taxes and promote growth.
Torgyan said all but absolute fringe political parties in Hungary support European and NATO integration.
"Just look at a map of our country and then you see immediately that there are borders which cannot be defended," he said.
"After 1945 we were pushed to join the nations of the Soviet Union and they destroyed what we had built. Now we want to restore our European relations because we are in the geographic centre."

Whether the right and centre-right will have the opportunity to lead a European-linked Hungary into the next century will depend a lot on the alliances that are worked out between now and the elections, due to be held by May 1998, analysts said.
"Sometimes the media a bit overplays the significance of the changes (in the opinion polls)," said Szonda-Ipsos general mnanager Adam Levendel.
"The Socialists still have a strong natural organisation and are very strong among the intellectuals...The real question, in the next months, and the next year, will be the change in the situation."
